title: Citizenship Amendment
summary: Fast-tracks Indian citizenship for Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan who entered India on or before 31 December 2014. Muslims are not among the covered groups, which is the core of the controversy.
provisions: Six communities from three countries are no longer treated as “illegal migrants”.
Cut-off date: entry on or before 31 December 2014.
Residency needed for naturalisation cut to 5 years for these groups.
Sixth Schedule tribal areas of the North-East and Inner Line Permit areas are excluded.

votes.note: Introduced and passed the same day; the vote came around midnight.
A motion to send it to a Select Committee failed 92–113.

committee.note: The 2019 Bill went to no committee. Its 2016 predecessor was examined by a Joint Parliamentary Committee, then lapsed.

arguments_for.text: It gives refuge to religious minorities persecuted in neighbouring countries where Islam is the state religion.
“No Indian has anything to worry regarding this act” — it grants citizenship and takes none away.
It builds on a long-standing commitment to Partition-era minorities, and an earlier version was examined by a Joint Committee.

arguments_against.text: Granting citizenship by religion violates equality under Article 14 and secularism.
arguments_against.by: Indian Union Muslim League and other petitioners

arguments_against.text: Persecuted Muslim sects such as Ahmadis and Hazaras, and Tamils from Sri Lanka, are left out; combined with an NRC, it could leave Muslim citizens stateless.
It breaks the 1985 Assam Accord, which set a 1971 cut-off, and threatens Assam’s culture.

timeline.text: Introduced and passed in Lok Sabha, 311–80.
Rules notified, more than four years later.
Supreme Court listed final hearing of about 237–242 petitions for 5–12 May.

status.text: In force, with rules in use since March 2024. The constitutional challenge is before the Supreme Court; we found no verdict as of October 2026.

reflection.aye: You voted with the government. In the Rajya Sabha the margin was 20 votes — the closest of the four bills here.
reflection.no: You joined 105 Rajya Sabha members. Twenty more votes the other way would have tied it.
reflection.committee: You backed the Select Committee motion. It failed 92–113.
reflection.abstain: You stayed out. In a 125–105 vote, every abstention on one side mattered.

question: Should a country’s citizenship law ever name religions? And who decides — Parliament or the courts?
